poiNSA-desc:
The North Sea Alliance is a great idea, one that could bear powerful fruit. Led from Edinburgh, it binds Scotland, England, Ireland, Iceland, Greenland and Norway into a single bloc that commands the North Sea and the polar trade routes beyond it. Critics call it an offshoot of the long-collapsed NATO, and its growth diplomatic imperialism. Its leaders answer that they do not wish to tear Europe apart like the ideologues of Paris and Berlin, nor to look only to their own interests like Moscow. They claim to want a better Europe.

Its wealth comes from the sea and from beneath the ground: coal above all, gas and iron, rare earths, titanium and the fisheries of the North Atlantic. Its money comes from elsewhere. {{poiNSA003|Iceland shelters the fortunes}} of Europe's upper classes and corporations, siphoning Franco-Iberian and Eurasian taxes into the Alliance, and the great docks of {{poiNSA001|the Edinburgh ARK}} {{poiNSA004|move nearly everything that enters northern Europe}}.

For now it is an alliance crumbling from within, as old rivalries resurface and delusions of grandeur seep into its politics. {{poiNSA002|Scotland strives to build a future apart from England}}, but fears the chaos to its south and {{poiNSA006|English stubbornness}}. {{poiNSA005|England shudders and wails as it falls apart}}, {{poiNSA007|the vultures fighting over its heart}}. If those troubles can be overcome, the Alliance will grow as new members join, and live up to its name by claiming dominion over the North Sea.
poiNSA001-desc:
The mountains stand firm as the tides rise and fall far below, as they have since the dawn of time. Now the sea comes sweeping lives, towns and entire cities away, never to be seen again. Other peoples weep and give in to it. Scotland will not. It fights, for once, not with sword and rifle but with shovel and crane. Massive pipes pump the water away, and vast walls of steel and concrete reclaim from the depths what the sea has stolen.

Its answer to the drowning coasts is the ARKs. Taking their name from the biblical ark, they are great cities built upon the sea itself, each one meant to preserve humanity, an industrial monument of economy and skill and a hub of human traffic. The Edinburgh ARK stands complete, the London ARK is under construction, and Norway keeps lobbying for a Nordic ARK of its own. Everyone wants a place on an ark. As in every disaster, demand outweighs supply.
poiNSA002-desc:
Born to a shipping magnate in the port of Aberdeen, Duncan Hughes was something of an enigma when he first appeared on the political circuit roughly a decade ago. He was schooled at the Sturgeon Naval College and had an otherwise comfortable upbringing, but biographers attribute the quirks of his personality to his teenage years on his father's docks. His father insisted he work as an apprentice longshoreman to learn a work ethic, and the other dockhands had little regard for "a soft-handed boy underfoot". The experience left him jaded, but his father may have been right: today Hughes is known as a tireless man with little fear of difficult confrontations.

He was one of the first to acknowledge publicly how far the Alliance lagged behind the other world powers. As head of the Priority Development Committee, he secured many of the trade deals and alliances behind its swift industrial ramp-up, and he now leads Scotland as Prime Minister, and the Alliance with it.
poiNSA003-desc:
Assuming all things in this world are logical, the Republic of Iceland should not exist as an independent nation. It is a tiny island in a strategic location, from which whoever controls it can command much of the Arctic Ocean. Scotland is its protector, but Iceland keeps a great deal of autonomy within the Alliance.

Iceland is not rich, populous or militarily powerful, so it has turned to what the political scientist Akello Malinga calls the Alpine Method of running a state, named after the famously free and discreet economies of Padania and the formerly independent Switzerland. It makes most of its money by offering European companies a safe place to dodge taxes and regulations. The Eurasians and Franco-Iberians are particularly vexed, forced to watch their upper classes and corporations hide their wealth in Icelandic bank accounts. Round after round of sanctions has failed to stop it.
poiNSA004-desc:
The docks of the Edinburgh ARK are among the largest and busiest in Europe, and almost everything bound for northern Europe passes through them at some point. That has made them extremely profitable for smugglers. The state-of-the-art contraband and chemical detection systems somehow always seem to detect very little.

Corruption set in years ago. The Italian Mafia, the Dutch Kliek, the Russian Bratva and the English Firms all pay exorbitant bribes to move drugs and weapons into the British Isles. A crackdown with rotating anonymous inspectors only changed the method: now workers are bribed to report false positives instead. Journalists have found the rot reaching up to local politicians, who lean on dockworkers to flag foreign goods, German and Icelandic cod among them, to please working-class voters at home.
poiNSA005-desc:
In 2200, England is a starkly divided nation. The rot started as ignorance when the Thames began to climb, and the official response was to build a wall around it. By the time London was drowning, the wolves had revealed themselves. Parliament moved to Birmingham, and nearly a century of inefficient, contentious rule has followed. Petty issues consume days of debate, aid money disappears into the vices of lying MPs, and getting anything done is cause for national celebration. Same as it ever was, yet somehow worse.

When a limping England was admitted to the North Sea Alliance, the country breathed a sigh of relief and cut its military budget to prop up the economy, leaving its defence to its allies. The Republican Army still exists, but its equipment and methods are woefully outdated, and any attempt to fund it would meet fierce opposition. The vultures circle overhead, and England's fate rests on the shoulders of foreign powers.
poiNSA006-desc:
Barbara Taylor's New Labour Party scrambles to catch the pieces of a crumbling state, alongside its benefactors in the Scottish Highlands. A union worker before she entered politics, Taylor now heads a government that spends its time squabbling behind the walls of Birmingham, and she is the one the people blame for decades of failure. Her efforts to correct course may only tip the country over the edge.

New Labour preaches the Masterist creed: England can only survive if it pushes ahead with vigour and a stiff upper lip, recovering and remaking what remains. The Industrial Revolution was born in Birmingham, and Taylor hopes a Masterist revolution may yet march out of it too.
poiNSA007-desc:
Everyone in England blames someone else, and each of Taylor's rivals has a reason.

Cassie Kenney grew up in a Lancashire valley that flooded six times in a decade. Government inaction left her family without food, water or power, and her boyfriend was beaten to death by a starving teenager who robbed them and found an empty fridge. She blames neither the teenager nor the river, but the government and the Masterists who keep poisoning a land that is already sinking. She founded the Lancashire section of the Harmonist Spring Party, and a year later the whole party elected her its leader.

Nigel John-Hall, Republican Army veteran and founder of the Purist English Front, sees England as a bloated corpse defiled by machines, and is officially a terrorist. He says the government are the real terrorists. Arthur Burr, a fisherman's son who lost his trade to a Scottish industrial trawler and his hand to an industrial accident, rejects every faction and rallies the Cavaliers for no ideology and no foreign patron, only for England. And Peter Clement, a carpenter turned beloved host of the home improvement show Just the Job, co-leads the Advance party with the London lawyer Julia Salisbury on a platform of redistribution and welfare.
